questions.q: With n counting qubits, what is the resolution of a phase estimation measurement?
options: 1/2^n -- the spacing between the 2^n evenly spaced representable estimates on [0, 1)
Exactly 1, regardless of n
n bits of precision for free, with no relationship to the number of possible outcomes
1/n, decreasing linearly rather than exponentially with n
questions.explain: With n counting qubits there are N = 2^n possible outcomes k/N, so the spacing between adjacent representable values is 1/2^n.

questions.q: What happens to the resource cost of phase estimation when you go from n to n+1 counting qubits?
options: The largest power of U that must be applied doubles, since the new top counting qubit controls U^(2^n)
The cost increases by exactly one additional application of U, with no other change
The cost decreases, since fewer total gates are needed for higher precision
There is no cost increase; precision is free beyond the first qubit
questions.explain: Counting qubit k controls U^(2^k), so adding one more precision bit requires controlling U^(2^n) -- doubling the largest required power of U.

questions.q: In the θ = 0.3, n = 3 worked example, why is k = 2 (estimate 0.25) the most likely measurement outcome even though it has probability 57.75%, not 100%?
options: Because θ = 0.3 is not exactly representable with 3 bits, so the circuit is genuinely probabilistic, concentrating most but not all probability on the nearest grid point, with real leakage to neighbors like k=3 at 25.93%
Because the circuit was built incorrectly and would give 100% with a correct implementation
Because k = 2 is always the default measurement outcome regardless of θ
Because probabilities in phase estimation always sum to exactly 57.75% for any θ
questions.explain: θ = 0.3 doesn't land exactly on the n=3 grid, so unlike the exact θ=1/4 case from Lesson 11, probability spreads across multiple outcomes, with the nearest grid point getting the largest but not the full share.

questions.q: According to the standard formula n = m + ceil(log2(2 + 1/(2ε))), what is the purpose of the extra counting qubits beyond m?
options: They absorb probability leakage into non-nearest outcomes, so the m reported bits are correct with probability at least 1 - ε
They directly increase the number of reported precision bits beyond m
They are only needed when ε = 0
They replace the need for controlled-U gates in the circuit
questions.explain: The extra qubits beyond m are padding that pushes probability leakage down, guaranteeing the m bits actually reported are correct with the desired confidence 1 - ε.

questions.q: Compared to the θ = 1/4, n = 2 example from Lesson 11, what makes the θ = 0.3, n = 3 example fundamentally different?
options: θ = 1/4 lands exactly on the n=2 grid giving a deterministic result (probability 1.0), while θ = 0.3 does not land exactly on the n=3 grid, producing a genuine probability spread across multiple outcomes
θ = 0.3 uses fewer counting qubits than θ = 1/4, making it less precise
Both examples are mathematically identical once normalized
θ = 1/4 requires more controlled-U applications than θ = 0.3
questions.explain: The key distinction is exact vs. non-exact representability on the measurement grid: 1/4 fits exactly in 2 bits (deterministic outcome), while 0.3 does not fit exactly in 3 bits (probabilistic spread).
